intro: って is the spoken shortcut for と and という: it holds something up in quotation marks. Either you pass on words ("he said that...", "I hear that..."), or you hold up a thing by its name to ask about it or comment on it ("Japanese, it's hard, isn't it?"). What comes after it tells you which: a verb of saying or thinking, or nothing at all, means a quote; a comment or a question about the thing means a topic.

skills.rule: In casual speech, put って after quoted words or thoughts where writing would use と (or という before a noun); on its own at the end of a sentence it means "I hear that, apparently".
skills.explain:
って replaces quoting と in conversation: 田中さんは来ないって言ってた (Tanaka said he isn't coming). It works with 言う, 思う, 聞く, 書いてある and the like, and with or without 「 」. Before a noun it replaces という: 駅で待ってるってメール (a text saying they're waiting at the station), 山田さんって人 (someone called Yamada).

The verb of saying is often dropped. A sentence that ends in って passes on what you heard: 明日は雨だって (apparently it'll rain tomorrow), 来られないって (he says he can't come). For this hearsay use a noun or na-adjective keeps だ: 休みだって, 静かだって. Without だ, 休みって sounds like the start of a topic.

って belongs to speech and casual writing such as messages. In formal writing and careful speech use と and という.
patterns: [plain-form clause] って 言う / 思う / 聞く
[noun / na-adj] だって。  hearsay keeps だ

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんは来[こ]ない{って}言[い]ってたよ。
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]だ{って}。
examples.en: Apparently it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 「すぐ行[い]く」{って}母[はは]に伝[つた]えて。
examples.en: Tell Mum I'm coming right away.

examples.jp: 駅[えき]で待[ま]ってる{って}メールが来[き]た。
examples.en: I got a message saying they're waiting at the station.

examples.jp: 山田[やまだ]さん{って}人[ひと]、知[し]ってる?
examples.en: Do you know someone called Yamada?

contrast.note: Same quoting job, but と is neutral and fits writing and formal speech: 来ないと言いました. と cannot end a sentence as hearsay and cannot link straight to a noun (来ないとメール is wrong); って can do both.
English "say X" tempts learners to use を for the quoted words. を marks a noun object such as 名前を言う or 嘘を言う; quoted words and clauses always take って or と.
If what follows is a comment on the thing (難しい, 何?, どう?) rather than a verb of saying, って is the casual topic, not a quote: 日本語って難しい is "Japanese is hard", not "someone said Japanese".

mistakes.bad: 田中[たなか]さんは「行[い]かない」{を}言[い]ってた。
mistakes.good: 田中[たなか]さんは「行[い]かない」{って}言[い]ってた。
mistakes.note: Quoted words are not a direct object. Mark them with って (casual) or と.

mistakes.bad: 山田[やまだ]さん{と}人[ひと]、知[し]ってる?
mistakes.good: 山田[やまだ]さん{って}人[ひと]、知[し]ってる?
mistakes.note: と cannot link a name or a clause straight to a noun. Casual って (or という) can.

skills.tip: Is there a verb of saying, thinking or hearing after the blank, or does the sentence end there with reported news? Casual って.

skills.rule: In casual speech, X って sets X up as the topic so you can define it, ask about it or comment on its nature: "X, (it's / what is it)?"
skills.explain:
Here って stands where は would stand, with a flavour of "this X we're talking about": 日本語って難しいね (Japanese is hard, isn't it?), これって何? (what is this?), 猫って本当によく寝るね (cats really do sleep a lot). It is typical for asking what something is or means (「積読」ってどういう意味?) and for general remarks about what someone or something is like (田中さんって優しいよね).

The comment after it is a description, a judgement or a question. It is not a plain report of a new event: "the bus has come" is バスが来た, never バスって来た, because a new event is marked with が.

って as topic is spoken and friendly. It mixes easily with です / ます in everyday talk (東京って家賃が高いんですか), but in writing, presentations and formal speech use は.
patterns: [noun] って 何 / どう / どういう意味?

examples.jp: 日本語[にほんご]{って}難[むずか]しいね。
これ{って}何[なん]ですか。
田中[たなか]さん{って}本当[ほんとう]に優[やさ]しいよね。
examples.en: Tanaka is really kind, don't you think?

examples.jp: 東京[とうきょう]{って}家賃[やちん]が高[たか]いんですか。
猫[ねこ]{って}よく寝[ね]るね。
examples.en: Cats really sleep a lot, don't they?

examples.jp: 「積読[つんどく]」{って}どういう意味[いみ]?

contrast.note: は is the neutral topic for every register. って gives the same sentence a conversational, curious or exclaiming tone, and only belongs in speech and casual messages.
が marks a subject as new information, such as a fresh event or the answer to "who / which": バスが来た, 田中さんが来た. って never does this; it only sets up something to comment on.
Look at what follows. 言う / 思う / 聞く after the blank: a quote. A description or question about the thing: the topic. Quote: 難しいって言った. Topic: 日本語って難しい.

mistakes.note: Something you have just seen happen is new information and takes が. って only sets up a topic to describe or ask about.

mistakes.bad: 本研究[ほんけんきゅう]{って}三年間[さんねんかん]のデータに基[もと]づく。
mistakes.good: 本研究[ほんけんきゅう]{は}三年間[さんねんかん]のデータに基[もと]づく。
mistakes.note: Topic って is spoken. In writing and formal speech use は.

skills.tip: Could you say it as "X, what's that like?" with a chatty tone and no verb of saying? Topic って, and は if the setting is formal.
